turkei-i-7-2-18.summary: In the autumn of 1547 Henry II, king for six months, sent his pantler, the sieur d’Huyson, to Constantinople with a letter of credence for Suleiman and instructions: join the truce that Charles V and Ferdinand had just made with the Porte, but have the king’s allies — the Swiss first — included in it, and expose imperial bad faith. Ferdinand’s resident in Constantinople, Giovanni Maria Malvezzi, got hold of the text, translated it back “from Turkish into Latin, word for word” and sent it to Vienna in cipher, together with a second, longer letter and a third, carried by a captain, about the Diet of Augsburg and asking for the Ottoman fleet. No earlier decipherment of the cipher is known; the archive's catalogue marks it not deciphered.
turkei-i-7-2-18.en:
Below {is} the copy of the letter of credence carrie{d} {by} ‹…› of the ‹…› [of the] Grand Signor, namely:

Most serene and most invincible Emperor of the Ottomans, lord, lord Sultan Suleiman, my dearest brother, greeting, the feeling of affection, all good fortune and continual increase of felicity. Most serene prince and dearest brother, we let you know that this nobleman, sincerely dear to us, our pantler named Duson, we have sent with our letters to [your] court ‹…›, that he may go as soon as possible to his court with our ambassador Gabriel de Ramon ‹…› on great matters that must be told by word of mouth; [Your Highness] is to give him undoubted faith, as if I were present in person. These matters, Most Serene, will also profit us greatly afterwards; take care to fare well and to live long and happily; and, {in its place}, Henry, King of France.

system: Malvezzi’s cipher alphabet: homophonic graphic signs (two to four per letter, numbers for double letters), nulls (syllables Dac, Der, Dam… and whole Latin words cum, etiam, porro), a few code words (Bi = King of France, Ras = the Sultan, Ab = the French)
